claim: This is the first in vitro study of the Min system in fully confined three-dimensional chambers that are lithography-defined, lipid-bilayer coated and isolated through pressure valves.
source: Here we present the first in vitro study of the Min system in fully confined three-dimensional chambers that are lithography-defined, lipid-bilayer coated and isolated through pressure valves.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this is the first study of its kind with these specific characteristics.

claim: Three typical dynamical behaviors occur in the chambers dependent on geometrical parameters: pole-to-pole oscillations, spiral rotations, and traveling waves.
source: We identify three typical dynamical behaviors that occur dependent on the geometrical chamber parameters: pole-to-pole oscillations, spiral rotations, and traveling waves.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Min-protein spiral rotations govern the larger part of the geometrical phase diagram.
source: We establish the geometrical selection rules and show that, surprisingly, Min-protein spiral rotations govern the larger part of the geometrical phase diagram.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by the phase diagram data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Confinement reduces the characteristic wavelength of the Min patterns.
source: Confinement as well as an elevated temperature reduce the characteristic wavelength of the Min patterns
evidence: This is supported by wavelength measurements comparing 2D surfaces to 3D confined chambers shown in Figure 6.

claim: Elevated temperature reduces the characteristic wavelength of the Min patterns.
source: Confinement as well as an elevated temperature reduce the characteristic wavelength of the Min patterns
evidence: This is supported by wavelength measurements at room temperature versus 37°C shown in Figure 6.

claim: Even for confined chambers with bacterial-level viscosity, the patterns retain a ~5 times larger wavelength than in vivo.
source: although even for confined chambers with a bacterial-level viscosity, the patterns retain a ~5 times larger wavelength than in vivo.
evidence: This is based on wavelength measurements in high viscosity conditions compared to known in vivo values.

claim: The Min protein system determines the localization of the division site in a wide range of bacterial cells.
source: The Min protein system determines the localization of the division site in a wide range of bacterial cells (Loose et al., 2011b; Lutkenhaus, 2012; Shih and Zheng, 2013; Rowlett and Margolin, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In Escherichia coli, Min proteins dynamically oscillate from pole-to-pole on a typical time scale of about 1 min.
source: In Escherichia coli (E. coli), Min proteins dynamically oscillate from pole-to-pole on a typical time scale of about 1 min (Raskin and de Boer, 1999; Hu and Lutkenhaus, 1999; Hale et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Reaction-diffusion mechanisms were invoked to explain Min oscillations.
source: Reaction-diffusion mechanisms were invoked in order to explain these oscillations (Kruse et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: The Min system is one of the most prominent examples of intracellular pattern formation in biology.
source: as of today, the Min system is one of the most prominent examples of intracellular pattern formation in biology (Soh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: MinD is an ATPase that can bind the plasma membrane through a short amphipathic peptide in a cooperative manner.
source: MinD, an ATPase that can bind the plasma membrane through a short amphipathic peptide (Hu and Lutkenhaus, 2003; Szeto et al., 2003) in a cooperative manner (Mileykovskaya et al., 2003; Renner and Weibel, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental work.

claim: MinD can bind the membrane in the ADP-bound form.
source: a recent work showed that MinD can also bind the membrane in the ADP-bound form (Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent experimental work.

claim: MinE is recruited to the membrane by MinD and induces MinD's ATPase activity causing MinD to be released from the membrane.
source: MinE, a protein that is recruited to the membrane by MinD (Ma et al., 2003), upon which it induces MinD's ATPase activity causing MinD to be released from the membrane (Hu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: MinE can persist on the membrane after MinD detachment.
source: Several authors showed that MinE can persist on the membrane after MinD detachment (Loose et al., 2011a; Park et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: MinE can interact with the membrane by itself.
source: or can even interact with the membrane by itself (Hsieh et al., 2010; Shih et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: MinC is recruited to the membrane by MinD and is released from MinD after MinE binding.
source: MinC protein is also recruited to the membrane by MinD, but, due to overlap binding with MinE, is released from MinD after MinE binding (Hu et al., 2003; Ma et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: MinC is the sole member of the Min system that directly interacts with the division apparatus.
source: While MinC is the sole member of the system that directly interacts with the division apparatus (Hu et al., 1999; Cordell et al., 2001; Dajkovic et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Only MinD and MinE are needed to form dynamical pole-to-pole oscillations in E. coli cells.
source: Thus, only MinD and MinE are needed in order to form dynamical pole-to-pole oscillations in E. coli cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statements about MinC being a passive hitchhiker and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: In filamentous E. coli cells, a dynamic series of Min bands with a characteristic length of ∼8 µm was observed.
source: When cells were grown as filaments, a dynamic series of Min bands with a characteristic length of ∼8 µm was observed (Raskin and de Boer, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: In filamentous cells grown at different temperatures, the Min length scale did not change but the temporal period of oscillations decreased according to an Arrhenius law.
source: When the filamentous cells were grown at different temperatures, this length scale did not change but the temporal period of the oscillations decreased according to an Arrhenius law (Touhami et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: In oval-shape cells, the Min system preferentially oscillated along the longest axis.
source: Likewise, in oval-shape cells, the Min system preferentially oscillated along the longest axis (Corbin et al., 2002; Shih et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: In rounded rodA-amber-mutation cells, the oscillation direction moved chaotically from one spot along the membrane to another.
source: in rounded rodA-amber-mutation cells, the oscillation direction moved chaotically from one spot along the membrane to another.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from previous work.

claim: Chaotic oscillations were observed when cells adopted aberrant shapes upon getting squeezed into slits smaller than their natural width.
source: A similar mode of chaotic oscillations was also observed when cells adopted aberrant shapes upon getting squeezed into slits smaller than their natural width (Männik et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: In Y-shaped E. coli cells, a sequence of oscillation nodes along the cell arms was observed that depended on the relative length of the Y shape arms.
source: In addition, when E. coli cells were mutated to form a Y shape, a sequence of oscillation nodes along the cell arms was observed that depended on the relative length of the Y shape arms (Varma et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The Min system can adapt to cell geometry and modify its dynamical behavior accordingly.
source: These results show that the Min system can adapt to the cell geometry and modify its dynamical behavior accordingly.
evidence: This is inferred from the collection of observations about Min behavior in different cell geometries.

claim: In sculpted E. coli cells of various rectangular and square shapes, the Min system behavior was characterized by a typical length scale of 3–6 µm.
source: In a recent example, Wu et al. sculpted E. coli cells into various rectangular and square shapes. They found that the Min system behavior was characterized by a typical length scale of 3–6 µm.
evidence: This is supported by reference to previous experimental work by Wu et al.

claim: The choice for a particular Min pattern is governed by the symmetries of the cell shape, its aspect ratio, and its size.
source: In addition, they showed that the choice for a particular Min pattern was governed by the symmetries of the cell shape, its aspect ratio, and its size.
evidence: This is supported by reference to previous experimental work by Wu et al.

claim: A variety of Min patterns were observed in sculpted cells, including rotational, transversal, and longitudinal modes.
source: Consequentially, a variety of Min patterns were observed, including rotational, transversal, and longitudinal modes (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: In vitro reconstitution of the Min system on supported lipid membranes significantly advanced the understanding of its dynamical mechanism.
source: In parallel with these cell-biology studies, in vitro reconstitution of the Min system on supported lipid membranes (SLB) significantly advanced the understanding of its dynamical mechanism (Loose et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: On 2D SLBs much larger than the typical length scale of Min patterns, Min proteins exhibit patterns grouped into rotating spirals and traveling waves.
source: On two-dimensional (2D) SLBs that are much larger than the typical length scale of the Min patterns, instead of oscillations, the Min proteins exhibit patterns that can be grouped into two classes: rotating spirals and traveling waves.
evidence: This is supported by reference to previous in vitro work.

claim: Traveling waves were formed when bands that emanated from two counter-rotating spirals collided.
source: In general, traveling waves were formed when bands that emanated from two counter-rotating spirals collided.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from in vitro experiments.

claim: The wavelength of traveling waves on 2D SLBs was very large, between 65–100 µm, and depended on the ratio of MinD to MinE concentration.
source: Importantly, the wavelength of the traveling waves was very large, between 65–100 µm, and depended on the ratio of MinD to MinE concentration.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from in vitro experiments.

claim: When the Min system is reconstituted in vitro, it exhibits pattern-formation behavior with a typical spatial dimension about an order of magnitude larger than observed in vivo.
source: Thus, when the Min system is reconstituted in vitro, it exhibits a pattern-formation behavior with a typical spatial dimension that is about an order of magnitude larger than the one observed in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing in vitro wavelengths (65-100 µm) to in vivo length scales (~8 µm).

claim: Under limiting concentration conditions, the Min system reconstituted in vitro exhibited unique patterns including a bursting type.
source: Interestingly, when the Min system was reconstituted under limiting concentration conditions, unique patterns, in particular a bursting type, were observed (Vecchiarelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Bursting patterns under limiting concentration conditions might be more closely related to the behavior of the Min system in vivo.
source: It was suggested that these patterns might be more closely related to the behavior of the Min system in vivo.
evidence: This is a suggestion from previous work cited.

claim: On rectangular patches of flat SLB separated by gold barriers, Min waves propagated in a direction that depended on the aspect ratio of the patch.
source: For example, when rectangular patches of flat surface SLB were separated one from the other with gold barriers that were much larger than the characteristic size of the Min dynamics in vitro (∼100 μm), Min waves propagated in a direction that depended on the aspect ratio of the patch (Schweizer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Min waves can be oriented within an SLB if parallel grooves are molded into the surface.
source: Similarly, Min waves can be oriented within an SLB if parallel grooves are molded into the surface (Zieske et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The geometry-selection rules found in in vitro experiments do not correspond to those observed in vivo.
source: However, the geometry-selection rules that were found in these in vitro experiments do not correspond to the ones that were observed in vivo (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between in vitro and in vivo observations with citation.

claim: Using partly confined fabricated reaction chambers, Min pole-to-pole oscillations as well as double and triple-band standing waves were reproduced, similar to patterns in filamentous E. coli.
source: Recently, utilizing partly confined fabricated reaction chambers, Zieske and Schwille were able to reproduce Min pole-to-pole oscillations as well as double and triple-band standing waves, similar to the patterns observed in filamentous E. coli (Zieske and Schwille, 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: In grooves shaped like dividing bacteria, Min proteins stochastically distributed between the two sides of the grooves, similar to distribution in E. coli mother cell progenies.
source: Similarly, Zieske et al. showed that when grooves had a shape similar to that of dividing bacteria at the last division stage, the Min proteins stochastically distributed between the two sides of the grooves. This observation is similar to the way that Min proteins are distributed between the two progenies of an E. coli mother cell (Di Ventura and Sourjik, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: In vitro Min oscillations were stable only when the groove width was much smaller than the in vitro wavelength of the waves.
source: However, these in vitro Min oscillations were stable only when the groove width was much smaller than the in vitro wavelength of the waves.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from previous in vitro work.

claim: When the overall bulk diffusivity of the proteins was decreased by a factor of 10, the Min wavelength was only marginally reduced.
source: For example, when the overall bulk diffusivity of the proteins was decreased by a factor of 10, the Min wavelength was, surprisingly, only marginally reduced (Schweizer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: On the outer side of giant unilamellar vesicles, both the wavelength and wave velocity of Min dynamics increased considerably relative to behavior on an SLB.
source: In contrast, when the Min dynamics was studied on the outer side of giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs), both the wavelength and wave velocity increased considerably relative to the behavior on an SLB (Martos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The 4-fold increase in diffusion rate of Min protein on GUVs membrane was suggested to be responsible for increased wavelength and velocity.
source: It was suggested that the 4-fold increase in the diffusion rate of the Min protein on the GUVs membrane was responsible for this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a suggestion from previous work cited.

claim: Increasing salt concentration or the ratio of anionic to natural phospholipids resulted in a reduction in the size of Min bands.
source: Concerning the reaction rates, by increasing the salt concentration or the ratio of anionic to natural phospholipids, Vecchiarelli et al. observed a reduction in the size of the Min bands (Vecchiarelli et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The reduction in Min band size by increasing salt or anionic lipids was attributed to different affinity of MinE to the membrane under these conditions.
source: which they attributed to the different affinity of MinE to the membrane under these conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation from previous work cited.

claim: Increasing cardiolipin concentration in the SLB to 70% molar ratio resulted in a decreased wavelength to about 25 µm.
source: Similarly, Zieske and Schwille observed a decreased wavelength to a value of about 25 µm by increasing the concentration of a negatively charged lipid, cardiolipin, in the SLB to an (unphysiologically high) molar ratio of 70% (Zieske and Schwille, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Even the reduced wavelength of 25 µm at 70% cardiolipin is still much larger than the characteristic ∼5 µm size scale measured in vivo.
source: Note that even this reduced value is still much larger than the characteristic ∼5 µm size scale measured in vivo.
evidence: This is a comparison between in vitro and in vivo measurements.

claim: Many mathematical models have been constructed for the Min system over the years.
source: Over the years, many mathematical models have been constructed for the Min system (Meinhardt and de Boer, 2001; Huang and Wingreen, 2004; Meacci and Kruse, 2005; Fischer-Friedrich et al., 2007; Arjunan and Tomita, 2010; Hoffmann and Schwarz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work.

claim: Each Min model postulated a somewhat different molecular mechanism and was able to reproduce several observed Min phenomena for certain parameter values.
source: Each of them postulated a somewhat different molecular mechanism and was able to reproduce several of the observed Min phenomena for certain values of the model's parameters.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of theoretical modeling with citations.

claim: The ability of Min models to explain all Min behaviors and robustness to parameter changes was less well considered.
source: However, the ability to explain all Min behaviors and the robustness to changes in the parameters was less well considered.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the state of theoretical modeling.

claim: The ability of Min models to gap the in vitro and in vivo behavior was not given much attention.
source: In particular, the ability to gap the in vitro and in vivo behavior of the system was not given much attention.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the state of theoretical modeling.

claim: Bonny et al. claimed they were able to bridge the gulf between in vitro and in vivo Min behavior.
source: Recently, Bonny et al. claimed that they were able to bridge this gulf (Bonny et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Bonny et al. could only reproduce in vivo oscillations and in vitro surface waves for reaction parameters that differed by several orders of magnitude between the two cases.
source: However, they were only able to reproduce the in vivo oscillations and in vitro surface waves for reaction parameters that were different in both cases over several orders of magnitudes, and the experimental basis for this variation remained unclear.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous theoretical work with citation.

claim: The best Min model to date was developed by Halatek and Frey, based on a previous model by Huang and Wingreen.
source: To date, the best Min model was developed by Halatek and Frey, based on a previous model by Huang and Wingreen (Huang et al., 2003; Halatek and Frey, 2012; Thalmeier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The Halatek and Frey model is able to reproduce most in vivo experimental results over a wide range of geometries and conditions.
source: This model is able to reproduce most of the in vivo experimental results over a wide range of geometries and conditions (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The ability of the Halatek and Frey model to reproduce Min behavior in vitro was not yet reported.
source: The ability of this model to reproduce the Min behavior in vitro was, however, not yet reported.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: One reason for lack of theoretical ability to reproduce all observed Min behaviors is the lack of comprehensive experimental results for in vitro behavior under a wide range of geometrical confinements.
source: One reason for the lack of theoretical ability to reproduce all observed Min behaviors using a single set of parameters is the lack of comprehensive experimental results for the in vitro behavior of Min proteins under a wide range of geometrical confinements.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the current study.

claim: Zieske and Schwille took first steps toward studying Min in confined compartments.
source: First steps in this direction were taken by Zieske and Schwille (Zieske and Schwille, 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Zieske and Schwille's compartments were only semi-confined and mainly probed the system for compartments much narrower than the typical Min wavelength.
source: However, their compartment were only semi-confined and they probed the system behavior mainly for compartments that were much narrower than the typical Min wavelength
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work with citations.

claim: A full description of geometrical selection rules for the Min system in confined chambers, especially the relation between in vitro oscillations and traveling waves, is still missing.
source: and hence, a full description of the geometrical selection rules for the Min system in confined chambers, and especially the relation between in vitro oscillations and in vitro traveling waves, is still missing.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature and motivation for the current study.

claim: The microfluidic chips are composed of two stacked PDMS layers.
source: We fabricated microfluidic chips that are composed of two stacked PDMS layers (see Figure 1a–c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 to Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claim: The bottom layer had rectangular chambers with height of ∼2.4 µm and lateral dimensions ranging from 10 × 10 µm to 60 × 80 µm.
source: The bottom layer had structures of three different heights: (i) Rectangular chambers with height of ∼2.4 µm and lateral dimensions ranging from 10 × 10 µm to 60 × 80 µm (blue part in Figure 1b)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claim: The bottom layer had reservoir channels with height of ∼30 µm and width of 100 µm.
source: (ii) Reservoir channels with height of ∼30 µm and width of 100 µm (red part in Figure 1b)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claim: The bottom layer had thin connector channels with height of ∼0.9 µm and width of ∼0.9 µm that connect the reservoirs and chambers.
source: (iii) thin connectors channels with height of ∼0.9 µm and width of ∼0.9 µm (green part in Figure 1c) that connect the reservoirs and the chambers.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claim: The upper layer of the device consisted of air-filled PDMS channels that served as pneumatic pressure valves.
source: The upper layer of the device consisted of air-filled PDMS channels that were aligned directly above the reservoir channels and connected to a high-pressure argon line thus serving as pneumatic pressure valves (Unger et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to the valve technology.

claim: Upon increasing the pressure of the air-filled channels, the ceiling of the lower layer deflected downward and closed the entrance to the connector lines.
source: Upon increasing the pressure of the air-filled channels in the upper layer, the ceiling of the lower layer (thickness ∼20 µm) deflected downward above the reservoir channels and closed the entrance to the connector lines.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of valve operation.

claim: The design allowed spatial isolation of the central PDMS chambers from the rest of the chip to obtain totally isolated 3D confined volumes.
source: Using this design, we were able to spatially isolate the central PDMS chambers (blue in Figure 1b) from the rest of the chip and to obtain totally isolated 3D confined volumes for studying the Min patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: A continuous SLB was formed on all the inner walls of the chambers after flushing with SUVs and incubating for ∼1 hr.
source: After the device was flushed with SUVs and incubated for ∼1 hr, a nice continuous SLB was formed on all the inner walls of the chambers (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The feature of microchambers covered by an SLB from all sides distinguishes this approach from previous studies that reconstituted Min proteins in fabricated structures.
source: This feature of our microchambers that are covered by an SLB from all sides is what distinguishes our approach from previous studies that reconstituted Min proteins in fabricated structures (Loose et al., 2008; Ivanov and Mizuuchi, 2010; Schweizer et al., 2012; Martos et al., 2015; Zieske and Schwille, 2013; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014; Zieske and Schwille, 2014; Vecchiarelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a key distinguishing feature with citations to previous work.

claim: Upon closing the pressure valves, truly confined chambers were obtained in the microfluidic devices.
source: These results corroborated that upon closing the pressure valves, we obtained truly confined chambers in our microfluidic devices.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from quality control experiments.

claim: In most cases, the Min proteins showed a defined pattern in each chamber that was stable for the duration of movie acquisition (∼10 min).
source: In most of the cases, the Min proteins showed a defined pattern in each chamber that was stable for the duration of the movie acquisition (∼10 min).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The typical time to reestablish the Min zone in the microchambers was 1−5 min.
source: As can be seen from Figure 1d–f, the typical time it took to reestablish the Min zone in these microchambers was 1−5 min.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in the figures.

claim: The large majority of observed patterns (>95%) could be readily classified into oscillations, traveling waves, or rotations.
source: The large majority of observed patterns (>95%) could be readily classified in these three categories.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: Clear relations exist between the geometry of the chamber and the observed dynamical Min behavior.
source: As can be seen, clear relations exist between the geometry of the chamber and the observed dynamical Min behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Rotational patterns appear as the majority for chambers with small aspect ratio.
source: (i) Rotational patterns appear as the majority for chambers with small aspect ratio (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: As the chamber aspect ratio increases, the probability to obtain rotational behavior decreases.
source: As the chamber aspect ratio increases, the probability to obtain rotational behavior decreases
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data in Figure 3a.

claim: For chambers with an aspect ratio larger than 2.8, rotational behavior was hardly observed.
source: and for chambers with an aspect ratio larger than 2.8, we hardly observed rotational behavior in our chambers.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Oscillatory behavior predominantly appears when the chamber width is small (∼10 µm).
source: (ii) Oscillatory behavior predominantly appears when the chamber width is small (∼10 µm) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Traveling waves mainly appear if the chamber length is relatively large.
source: (iii) Traveling waves mainly appear if the chamber length is relatively large (Figure 3c)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The prevalence of traveling waves increases as the chamber length increases.
source: and their prevalence increases as the chamber length increases.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data in Figure 3c.

claim: If the chamber area is relatively large, the prevalence of obtaining traveling waves increases.
source: Similarly, if the chamber area is relatively large the prevalence of obtaining a traveling waves increases (see. Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: For large chamber areas, the confined chambers reflect the surface waves that were observed on unbound SLBs.
source: For these large areas, the confined chambers reflect the surface waves that were observed on unbound SLBs (Loose et al., 2008; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations to previous work.

claim: The clear relation between chamber geometry and dynamical Min patterns unambiguously proves that confinement sets the rules for Min pattern formation.
source: The clear relation found between the chamber geometry and the dynamical Min patterns unambiguously proves that confinement sets the rules for Min pattern formation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The existence of connector lines in the setup adds only second-order effects.
source: It also supports the notion that the existence of the connector lines in our setup adds only second-order effects.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the clear geometry-pattern relationship.

claim: By using soft fabricated valves, geometrical selection rules of the Min system in truly confined 3D structures in vitro were extracted and studied for the first time.
source: Thus, by using the soft fabricated valves, we were able to extract and study, for the first time, the geometrical selection rules of the Min system in truly confined 3D structures in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a key achievement of the study.

claim: The phase diagram is nicely separated into three different regions: rotations, oscillations in narrow chambers, and traveling waves in large and long chambers.
source: As can be seen from Figure 4a, the phase diagram is nicely separated into three different regions: (i) The majority pattern is rotations; (ii) oscillations are the most prevalent pattern in narrow chambers, in line with previous observation in semi-3D-confined structures (Zieske and Schwille, 2013, 2014); and (iii) as expected (Loose et al., 2008, 2011a), the most prevalent behavior for large and long chambers is that of traveling waves.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4a with citations to previous work.

claim: In fully confined 3D chambers, a large part of the phase diagram is occupied by rotational behavior.
source: The most striking, and unexpected, result of this study is that in fully confined 3D chambers, a large part of the phase diagram is occupied by rotational behavior, i.e., Min patterns that rotate around a fixed point in a spiral fashion.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding from the phase diagram.

claim: When chambers become too narrow, rotational centers are less stable and oscillations are formed.
source: When the chambers becomes too narrow, these rotational centers are less stable, presumably due to reflection of the Min concentration front from the chamber boundaries, and oscillations are formed.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the phase diagram data.

claim: Oscillations appear to be a derivative phenomenon that results from destabilization of spiral rotating patterns by the chamber walls.
source: Oscillations thus appear to be a derivative phenomenon that results from destabilization of spiral rotating patterns by the chamber walls.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the phase diagram data.

claim: For very large areas, the interaction between multiple rotational centers equilibrates such that the stable behavior becomes a traveling wave.
source: In the other extreme, for very large areas, the interaction between multiple rotational centers will equilibrate in such a way that the stable behavior becomes a traveling wave.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the phase diagram data.

claim: The actual concentration of Min proteins in the chambers was significantly (∼factor 5) higher than the injected stock solution value.
source: As can be seen (Figure 5a), the actual concentration of the Min proteins in our chambers was significantly (∼factor 5 higher than the value for the injected stock solution.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5a based on GFP calibration measurements.

claim: A wide distribution of Min protein concentrations was observed in the chambers, particularly for MinE.
source: Furthermore, a wide distribution is observed, particularly for MinE.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the concentration measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: No relation was observed between chamber size and the measured concentration of Min proteins.
source: Note that we did not observe a relation between the chamber size and the measured concentration of the Min proteins.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the concentration measurements.

claim: The concentration of MinD in the chambers was 4.5 ± 0.5 µM (mean ± SD).
source: From these measurements we concluded that the concentration of MinD in our chambers was 4.5 ± 0.5 µM (mean ± SD)
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the GFP calibration measurements.

claim: The concentration of MinE in the chambers was 6 ± 3 µM.
source: the concentration of MinE 6 ± 3 µM
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the GFP calibration measurements.

claim: The average ratio of [MinE]/[MinD] in the chambers was 1.3 ± 0.5.
source: and the average ratio of [MinE]/[MinD] amounted to 1.3 ± 0.5.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the GFP calibration measurements.

claim: The wavelength of Min waves in confined chambers at room temperature was 43 ± 6 µM.
source: We measured a wavelength of 43 ± 6 µM at room temperature.
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The wavelength on 2D flat SLBs at room temperature was 78 ± 12 µM.
source: This value is significantly lower than the wavelength of 78 ± 12 µM (n = 30 for traveling waves that we measured on 2D flat SLBs using the exact same protein and lipid composition of the SLB as was used in our microchambers experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a.

claim: 3D full confinement of the Min system has a clear effect on the characteristic length scale of the system.
source: This shows that the 3D full confinement of the Min system has a clear effect not only on the geometry-selection properties, but also on the characteristic length scale of the system.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing wavelengths in 3D chambers versus 2D surfaces.

claim: The velocity of Min patterns in chambers at room temperature was 0.3 ± 0.1 µm/s.
source: inside the chambers we obtained a propagation velocity of 0.3 ± 0.1 µm/s
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The velocity of Min waves on flat SLB surfaces at room temperature was 0.6 ± 0.2 µm/s.
source: While on flat SLB surfaces we measured v = 0.6 ± 0.2 µm/s, similar to previous measured values (Loose et al., 2011a)
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b with citation to previous work.

claim: The reduced wavelength inside the chambers was accompanied by a reduced velocity.
source: The reduced wavelength inside the chambers was thus accompanied with a reduced velocity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing wavelengths and velocities.

claim: The measured viscosity of the crowding solution (4% PEG 8000, 4% Ficol 400, 4% BSA) is 9.9 ± 0.05 cP.
source: The measured viscosity of this solution is 9.9 ± 0.05 cP, i.e., one order of magnitude larger than that of water.
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result.

claim: The viscosity of the crowding solution is close to the estimated viscosity inside E. coli cells.
source: Though the exact viscosity inside E. coli cells is unknown, this value is close to the estimated one (Trovato and Tozzini, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Increasing the viscosity of the environment resulted in a factor 2 reduction of the wavelength from 43 ± 6 µm to 23 ± 4 µm.
source: Increasing the viscosity of the environment resulted in a factor 2 reduction of the wavelength from 43 ± 6 µm to 23 ± 4 µm.
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The reduction in wavelength with increased viscosity is comparable to the reduction observed by Martos et al. in the presence of 140 g/l Ficol.
source: This reduction in the wavelength is comparable to the reduction in wavelength that was observed by Martos et al. in the presence of 140 g/l Ficol (Martos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work with citation.

claim: A very large decrease of more than one order of magnitude in wave velocity was observed with increased viscosity, from 0.3 ± 0.1 µm to 0.02 ± 0.014 µm/s.
source: Next to the reduction in the wavelength, we observed a very large decrease, of more than one order of magnitude, in the wave velocity from 0.3 ± 0.1 µm to 0.02 ± 0.014 µm/s.
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The substantial decrease in velocity with increased viscosity is much larger than what was observed by Martos et al. and is probably related to the different constellations of 2D surfaces versus 3D confined microchambers.
source: Note that this substantial decrease in the velocity is much larger than what was observed by Martos et al. and is probably related to the different constellations of 2D surfaces (used by Martos et al.) in comparison to 3D confined microchambers (in this work).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation comparing to previous work with citation.

claim: The geometry selection properties of the Min system at 37°C are very similar to those observed at room temperature.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3d–f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, the geometry selection properties of the Min system at the elevated temperature of 37°C are very similar to those that were observed at room temperature (n = 198)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 3d-f.

claim: At low aspect ratio of chambers, the prevalence to obtain rotational patterns is high at 37°C and decreases as aspect ratio increases.
source: (i) at low aspect ratio of the chambers (L/W), the prevalence to obtain rotational patterns is high while it decreases as the aspect ratio increases
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data at 37°C.

claim: Oscillatory behavior is observed mainly for narrow chambers at 37°C.
source: (ii) oscillatory behavior is observed mainly for narrow chambers
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data at 37°C.

claim: Traveling waves become dominant for long and large chambers at 37°C.
source: (iii) traveling waves become dominant for long and large chambers.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data at 37°C.

claim: The wavelength at 37°C shows only a small decrease relative to room temperature, from 43 ± 6 µm to 37 ± 9 µm.
source: The wavelength at the elevated temperature (see Figure 6a, n = 34), shows only a small decrease relative to the wavelength at room temperature, that is from 43 ± 6 µm to 37 ± 9 µm (two sample t-test with different variance = 0.001 at β = 0.05).
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a with statistical test.

claim: For waves on flat 2D SLB surfaces, the wavelength reduced from 78 ± 12 at room temperature to 48 ± 6 µm at 37°C.
source: This contrasts the behavior of waves on flat 2D SLBs surfaces, for which we observed a much more profound effect (Figure 6a, n = 27). In this case the wavelength reduced from 78 ± 12 at room temperature to 48 ± 6 µm at 37°C.
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6a.

claim: In confined chambers, confinement is the major cause of reduced wavelength, with elevated temperature adding only a small further reduction.
source: These data thus show that, in confined chambers, confinement is the major cause of the reduced wavelength, with the elevated temperature adding only a small further reduction in the characteristic spatial scale of the system.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing wavelength data at different temperatures and confinement conditions.

claim: At T = 37°C, the velocity of Min patterns in chambers was v = 0.5 ± 0.3 µm/s.
source: At T = 37°C, the velocity v = 0.5 ± 0.3 µm/s (velocity for waves only v = 0.5 ± 0.1 µm/s n = 34).
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b.

claim: At T = 37°C, the velocity of waves on flat SLBs was v = 1.4 µm/s.
source: This compares to v = 1.4 µm/s (Figure 6b) for waves propagating on flat SLBs surfaces.
evidence: This is stated as a measurement result shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Similar to conditions in vivo, elevated temperature increases the velocity of Min propagation in vitro, doubling from 23°C to 37°C both on 2D surfaces and in 3D confinement.
source: Thus, similar to the conditions in vivo, where the period of the oscillations is inversely correlated with the temperature (Touhami et al., 2006), elevated temperature increases the velocity of the Min propagation in vitro, doubling from 23°C to 37°C both on 2D surfaces and in 3D confinement.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from velocity measurements with citation to in vivo work.

claim: In contrast to in vivo behavior, the in vitro wavelength is temperature dependent.
source: However, in contrast to the in vivo behavior, the in vitro wavelength is also temperature dependent.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from wavelength measurements comparing to in vivo observations.

claim: The viscosity of the bulk media changes only by a factor of 1.3 from 23°C to 37°C.
source: Since the viscosity of the bulk media change only by a factor of 1.3 from 23°C to 37°C
evidence: This is stated as a known physical property.

claim: The temperature effect on wavelength must be attributed to a change in one of the reaction parameters of the reaction-diffusion Min system.
source: we have to attribute these results to a change in one of the reaction parameters of the reaction-diffusion Min system.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data.

claim: There are different ways to modulate the different dynamical characteristics (wavelength and velocity) of the Min system.
source: We can conclude that there are different ways to modulate the different dynamical characteristics (wavelength and velocity) of the Min system.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Total confinement of the Min system within 3D chambers leads to three main types of patterns: rotational patterns in the form of spiral waves (majority), periodic oscillations (mainly if chamber width is small), and traveling waves (mainly if one dimension is larger than typical spatial length scale).
source: In this article, we have shown that total confinement of the Min system within 3D chambers leads to three main type of patterns: (i) rotational patterns in the form of spiral waves, which are the majority of the patterns found; (ii) periodic oscillations that occur mainly if the chamber width is small in comparison to the typical spatial length scale of the system in vitro; (iii) traveling waves that occur mainly if one of the dimensions of the chamber is larger than the typical spatial length scale of the system.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main findings.

claim: In microchambers, rotational behavior in the form of spiral waves contributes the largest fraction of the phase diagram.
source: In our microchambers, rotational behavior in the form of one or multiple adjacent spiral waves thus contributes the largest fraction of the phase diagram.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding from the phase diagram.

claim: Spiral waves are common in various biological and chemical reaction-diffusion processes such as Dictyostelium discoideum aggregation, calcium variations in Xenopus laevis oocytes, and the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction.
source: Spiral waves are common in various biological and chemical reaction-diffusion processes such as Dictyostelium discoideum aggregation, calcium variations in Xenopus laevis oocytes, and the famous Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction (see Epstein and Pojman, 1998 and references therein).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Spiral waves were observed for the Min system on flat SLBs.
source: They were also observed for the Min system on flat SLBs (Loose et al., 2008; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: For the BZ reaction, spiral waves were attributed to a Hopf bifurcation mechanism.
source: For example, for the BZ reaction, spiral waves were attributed to a Hopf bifurcation mechanism (Hagan, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: In nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems, several symmetry-breaking mechanisms may coexist in different parts of the parameter phase space, resulting in a plethora of static or dynamic patterns.
source: In addition, it is well known that in nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems, several symmetry-breaking-mechanisms may coexist in different parts of the parameter phase space and, as result, a plethora of static or dynamic patterns can emerge (Yang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: It is possible that in vitro Min patterns emanate from a different symmetry-breaking mechanism than Min oscillations in live cells despite the proteins being the same.
source: In light of this knowledge, it is well possible that in vitro Min patterns, in fact, emanate from a somehow different symmetry-breaking-mechanism than the Min oscillations in live cells despite the fact that the proteins are the same and the patterns share various similar characteristics with the in vivo case.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the observations.

claim: The existence of spirals in vitro and their abundance in confined microchambers, compared to their absence in vivo where pole-to-pole oscillations dominate, may be related to different symmetry-breaking mechanisms.
source: The existence of spirals in vitro and their abundance in our confined microchambers, when compared to their absence from in vivo observations where pole-to-pole oscillations dominate (Wu et al., 2015), may be related to this.
evidence: This is stated as speculation with citation to in vivo work.

claim: Spiral patterns were not stable in narrow chambers smaller than or equal to the characteristic 10 µm length scale of spirals.
source: We observed that the spiral patterns were found not to be stable in narrow chambers that are smaller than, or equal to, the characteristic 10 µm length scale of spirals.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Pole-to-pole oscillations are established as the chamber walls restrict spirals to form.
source: We observed that pole-to-pole oscillations are established as the chamber walls restrict spirals to form.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: In vitro oscillations appear to be a form of truncated spirals.
source: In other words, in vitro oscillations in fact appear to be a form of truncated spirals.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the observations.

claim: The data are the first to suggest that in vitro oscillations are truncated spirals.
source: These data are the first to suggest that in vitro oscillations are truncated spirals
evidence: This is stated as a novel interpretation.

claim: In vivo, spiral rotations were not observed.
source: Please note also that in vivo, spiral rotations were not observed (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous in vivo work.

claim: Spiral rotations were not suggested as the origin of the symmetry-breaking mechanism in theoretical works.
source: Neither were they suggested as the origin of the symmetry-breaking mechanism in theoretical works.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the theoretical literature.

claim: In vivo, pole-to-pole oscillations amount to the establishment of a polar zone that is replaced by a second polar zone near the opposite pole within a short time scale.
source: In vivo, the pole-to-pole oscillations amount to the establishment of polar zone that is replaced by a second polar zone near the opposite pole within a short time scale.
evidence: This is stated as a description of in vivo behavior.

claim: In vitro oscillations are more akin to a traveling wave that propagates toward one pole, then is replaced by a wave established near the chamber middle that propagates toward the opposite pole.
source: In contrast to this, in vitro oscillations are more akin to a traveling wave that propagates toward one pole, whereupon it is then replaced by a wave that is established close to the chamber middle and propagates toward the opposite pole
evidence: This is stated as a description of in vitro behavior observed in this study.

claim: Similar oscillation behavior to in vitro was observed in other reconstitution work.
source: Similar behavior was also observed in in vitro oscillations of other reconstitution work (Zieske and Schwille, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The difference in oscillation character between in vivo and in vitro may be the reason why steep in vitro Min gradients that would restrict FtsZ localization to a single ring could not be established.
source: This may also be the reason why steep in vitro Min gradients that would restrict FtsZ localization to a single ring could not have been established.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the observations.

claim: In vivo traveling waves represent a form of abnormal behavior which occurs if MinE function is impaired or in other anomalous cases.
source: Note that in all these cases, the in vivo traveling waves represent a form of abnormal behavior which occurs if the MinE function is impaired or in other anomalous cases.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of in vivo observations.

claim: In vitro, traveling waves can be a generic feature of the Min system.
source: This contrasts to the in vitro case, where traveling waves can be a generic feature of the Min system.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from in vitro observations.

claim: On flat 2D SLBs, spiral waves are not confined and waves from one center can travel long distances and interfere with waves from a second spiral center to form traveling waves.
source: First, on flat 2D SLBs the spirals waves are not confined and hence waves that emanate from one center can travel long distance and interfere with waves that emanate from a second spiral center to form traveling waves.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for traveling wave formation on 2D surfaces.

claim: In large chambers, the intrinsic Min pattern formation mechanism and reflection from chamber walls result in annihilation of spiral centers and establishment of traveling waves.
source: In our chambers, when their area became large, the intrinsic Min pattern formation mechanism and the reflection from the chambers walls resulted in the annihilation of spiral centers and the establishment of traveling waves, similar to the 2D case where boundaries are absent.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for traveling wave formation in large chambers.

claim: Due to the small surface-to-volume ratio in typical in vitro assays, the actual concentration of proteins on the membrane and the replenished reservoir is higher than in vivo.
source: However, due to the small surface-to-volume ratio in typical in vitro assays, the actual concentration of the proteins on the membrane and the replenished reservoir of new Min proteins is higher than in vivo (cf. the above section on Min concentration in the microchambers).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation with reference to the concentration measurements.

claim: The high protein concentration situation in vitro is qualitatively different from in vivo where cytosolic concentration drops to a low value during polar zone or Min band formation.
source: This situation is qualitatively different from the in vivo case where, during the formation of polar zone or a Min band, most of the MinD proteins are recruited to the membrane and the cytosolic concentration thus drops to a low value.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between in vitro and in vivo conditions.

claim: Vecchiarelli et al. suggested that in vitro spiral waves are related to high concentration of Min proteins, while reconstituting under limiting concentration conditions resulted in Min bursts reminiscent of behavior in cells.
source: Indeed, in a very recent publication, Vecchiarelli et al. suggested that in vitro spirals waves are related to high concentration of the Min proteins, while reconstituting the Min system under limiting concentration conditions resulted in a dynamical series of Min bursts that are reminiscent of the behavior in cells (Vecchiarelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: When MinE was replaced by membrane-binding deficient mutant MinE11–88, Min waves were supported at high protein concentration but bursting dynamics were absent.
source: Vecchiarelli et al. further checked the behavior of the Min proteins when MinE was replaced by a membrane-binding deficient mutant MinE11–88, and observed that in this case, Min waves were supported at high protein concentration, but bursting dynamics were absent.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Vecchiarelli et al.'s work.

claim: The observation with MinE11–88 was consistent with Zieske et al. where oscillations were not observed with a similar mutant MinE(Δ3–8).
source: This observation was consistent with the one of Zieske et al. (Zieske and Schwille, 2014) where oscillations were not observed with a similar mutant MinE(Δ3–8).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The interrelations between surface-to-volume ratio, protein concentration, confinement, and MinE binding to membrane determine the pattern formation mechanism in vitro.
source: Thus, it seems that the interrelations between several factors determine the pattern formation mechanism in vitro: the surface-to-volume ratio, the protein concentration, the confinement, and the binding of MinE to the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the discussion of various factors.

claim: The results with relatively high Min protein concentration support Vecchiarelli et al.'s conclusions about concentration effects.
source: Our results, with the relatively high Min protein concentration that we measured, support their conclusions.
evidence: This is stated as support for previous work based on the current study's measurements.

claim: Fully confining the Min system in 3D chambers with relatively small height enabled studying the system in conditions with a surface-to-volume ratio much larger than previously studied.
source: The fact that we fully confined the Min system in 3D chambers with a relatively small height enabled us to look on the behavior of the system in conditions with a surface-to-volume ratio that is much larger than previously studied.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Combined with measurements of total Min protein concentration, the results set a lower limit for protein concentration that still reproduces traveling waves, rotational spirals, or oscillations under these geometric conditions.
source: Combined with our measurements of the total Min protein concentration in the chambers, our results set a lower limit for the protein concentration that still reproduces traveling waves, rotational spirals, or oscillations under these geometric conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Bonny et al. were able to show traveling waves in their theoretical system by increasing Min concentration by 63% or by increasing the MinE to MinD ratio.
source: Indeed, Bonny et al. were able to show traveling waves in their theoretical system by increasing the Min concentration by 63% or by increasing the MinE to MinD ratio (Bonny et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: In chambers with high surface-to-volume ratio and high Min protein concentration, the cumulative effect of annihilation of multiple spirals and reflection from walls can result in traveling wave formation.
source: In our geometrical analysis of Min patterns selection, we showed that in chambers with high surface-to-volume ratio, and a high Min proteins concentration, the cumulative effect of annihilation of multiple spirals and of the reflection from the walls can result in the formation of traveling waves.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the geometrical analysis.

claim: A reduction in Min wavelength by a factor of two was observed in microchambers relative to 2D flat SLB.
source: We have observed a reduction in the Min wavelength by a factor of two in our microchambers relative to the case of 2D flat SLB.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Lateral confinement may be responsible for choosing dynamical modes with smaller wavelength.
source: First, the lateral confinement by itself may be responsible for choosing dynamical modes of the system with a smaller wavelength.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for wavelength reduction.

claim: Height reduction could change the balance between the reservoir of free Min proteins in solution relative to bound ones.
source: Second, the height reduction could change the balance between the reservoir of the free Min proteins in solution relative to the bound ones.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for wavelength reduction.

claim: Halatek and Frey suggested that reducing the volume of Min proteins above the surface will drive the typical wavelength to lower values.
source: Indeed, based on their model, Halatek and Frey recently suggested, that reducing the volume of Min proteins above the surface will drive the typical wavelength of the system to lower values (personal communication).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical prediction from personal communication.

claim: Thalmeier et al. showed theoretically that even in the absence of MinE, Arabidopsis thaliana MinD can form an intracellular gradient based on relations between bulk diffusion and nucleotide exchange rates, but only in highly confined spaces.
source: Similarly, it was shown theoretically by Thalmeier et al. (Thalmeier et al., 2016) that even in the absence of MinE, Arabidopsis thaliana MinD can form an intracellular gradient just based on the relations between the bulk diffusion and nucleotide exchange rates, but only in highly confined spaces.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: The observation that reducing chamber height is accompanied by reduction of both wavelength and wave velocity stresses the value of studying Min behavior in 3D confined spaces with high surface-to-volume ratio.
source: Thus, our observation that reducing the height of the chamber is accompanied by a reduction of both the wavelength and the wave velocity further stresses the value of our approach of studying the Min behavior in 3D confined spaces with a high surface-to-volume ratio.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion emphasizing the importance of the experimental approach.

claim: The chambers are 2.4 µm high, not much larger than the 1 µm diameter of an E. coli bacterium, yet the measured wavelength is an order of magnitude larger than the characteristic length scale observed in vivo.
source: We note, however, that our chambers are 2.4 µm high, not too much larger than the 1 µm diameter of an E. coli bacterium, and yet, we measured a wavelength that is an order of magnitude larger than the characteristic length scale observed in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an observation comparing chamber dimensions to bacterial dimensions and in vivo length scales.

claim: The Min wavelength decreased by a factor of 2 when medium viscosity was raised to 10 cP.
source: We have shown that two factors can lower the wavelength further. First, the Min wavelength decreased by a factor of 2 when the viscosity of the medium was raised to 10 cP, i.e., similar to that of cells and ten times larger than a regular buffer.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Even at high viscosity (10 cP), the wavelength was larger by a factor of ∼5 from the one measured in vivo.
source: Still, even at this high viscosity, the wavelength was larger by a factor of ∼5 from the one measured in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an observation comparing in vitro to in vivo measurements.

claim: The reduction in wavelength at high viscosity was accompanied by a very large reduction in wave propagation velocity.
source: In addition, the reduction in wavelength was accompanied by a very large reduction in the wave propagation velocity.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The measured velocity in highly viscous media was similar or even smaller than the one measured in vivo.
source: Note that the measured velocity in the highly viscous media was similar or even smaller than the one measured in vivo (Unai et al., 2009) (see also the supporting information in [Bonny et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to in vivo measurements with citations.

claim: It is unlikely that additional increases in viscosity can bring both the characteristic length scale and propagation velocity of the system in vitro to the in vivo values.
source: It is thus unlikely that additional increases in viscosity can bring both the characteristic length scale and the propagation velocity of the system in vitro to the in vivo values.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the viscosity experiments.

claim: Increasing temperature reduced the wavelength, with the effect being much larger for Min waves on flat SLBs than in 3D confined chambers.
source: Second, we showed that increasing the temperature also reduced the wavelength. The effect of the temperature on the characteristic wavelength was much larger for the Min waves on flat SLBs than in the 3D confined chambers.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Since diffusion rate does not change substantially between room temperature and 37°C, the temperature effect in 2D surface case is most likely the result of a change in one of the reaction parameters, probably ATP hydrolysis rate.
source: Since the diffusion rate does not change substantially between room temperature and 37°C (only a factor of 1.3, by the Einstein's relation), the temperature effect in the 2D surface case is most likely the result of a change in one of the reaction parameters, most probably the ATP hydrolysis rate.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the temperature effect.

claim: In microchambers, the main in vitro determinant of wavelength at elevated temperature is the geometrical confinement itself.
source: This situation is different in the microchambers. Our observations suggest that the main in vitro determinant of the wavelength at elevated temperature in confined spaces is the geometrical confinement itself.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the temperature experiments in chambers.

claim: Geometrical confinement forces the system to choose a reaction-diffusion mode with reduced wavelength which can only marginally be tuned further by increasing temperature.
source: In other word, geometrical confinement forces the system to choose a reaction-diffusion mode with a reduced wavelength which can only marginally be tuned further by increasing the temperature.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the confinement and temperature effects.

claim: In highly confined spaces, the effect of temperature on the characteristic scale of the Min system is largely diminished and is accounted by the small increase in diffusion rate.
source: Thus, in highly confined spaces the effect of temperature on the characteristic scale of the Min system is largely diminished, and is accounted by the small increase in diffusion rate.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the temperature experiments.

claim: The reduced length scale at elevated temperature was accompanied by an increase in wave velocity, in line with the in vivo case where oscillation period was smaller at high temperature.
source: It should be noted that the reduced length scale was accompanied by an increase, rather than a decrease, of the wave velocity. This observation is in line with the in vivo case where the oscillation period was smaller at high temperature.
evidence: This is stated as an observation comparing to in vivo behavior.

claim: The dynamical characteristics of the Min system contain several decoupled parameters, such as wavelength and velocity, that can be tuned in opposite directions.
source: Our results points out that the dynamical characteristics of the Min system contain several decoupled parameters, such as wavelength and velocity that can be tuned in opposite directions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: It is essential to study the dynamical parameters of the Min system in the context of 3D confined spaces with high surface-to-volume ratio.
source: It is thus essential to study their action in the context of 3D confined spaces with a high surface-to-volume ratio.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the importance of the experimental approach.

claim: Dynamical aspects of the Min system can be tuned in at least three different ways: by confinement, by changing temperature, and by reducing bulk viscosity.
source: We have shown that dynamical aspects of the system can be tuned in at least three different ways: by confinement, by changing the temperature, and by reducing the bulk viscosity.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: In 3D confined structures, even at elevated temperature or with high viscous media, the in vitro Min behavior did not quantitatively reproduce the in vivo one.
source: Yet, since in our 3D confined structures, even at elevated temperature or with high viscous media, the in vitro Min behavior did not quantitatively reproduce the in vivo one
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: A change of yet another dynamical parameter is probably necessary to reproduce in vivo behavior, possibly a change in concentration of one of the Min proteins or a change in one of the reaction rates.
source: probably a change of yet another dynamical parameter is necessary. This can be a simple thing like a change in the concentration of one of the Min proteins (Vecchiarelli et al., 2016) or a change in one of the reaction rates.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about what might be needed with citation.

claim: It is possible that yet another physical or biological mechanism contributes to the different symmetry breaking in vitro versus in vivo.
source: It is also possible that yet another physical or biological mechanism contributes to the different symmetry breaking in both cases.
evidence: This is stated as speculation.

claim: MinD increased the order of lipids and decreased their mobility in inverted inner E. coli membranes containing integral proteins more than in synthetic vesicles that are purely lipidic.
source: For example, MinD increased the order of the lipids and decreased their mobility in inverted inner E. coli membranes that contained integral proteins more than it does in synthetic vesicles that are purely lipidic (Mazor et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The Min system affects the association of inner-membrane peripheral proteins and interacts with some of them directly.
source: Similarly, the Min system affects the association of inner-membrane peripheral proteins and interacts with some of them directly (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: It is possible that a yet unidentified protein species is needed to reproduce the in vivo geometrical selection rules of the Min system in an in vitro environment.
source: It is thus possible that a yet unidentified protein species is needed in order to reproduce the in vivo geometrical selection rules of the Min system in an in vitro environment.
evidence: This is stated as speculation.

claim: The study found three main patterns in confined chambers: spiral rotations, oscillations and traveling waves.
source: To sum up, we have studied the geometry selection rules of the Min system in 3D fully confined chambers. We found three main patterns in these confined chambers: spiral rotations, oscillations and traveling waves.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main findings.

claim: Spiral behaviors were the most abundant in a large part of the phase diagram.
source: Spiral behaviors were the most abundant ones in a large part of the phase diagram
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the phase diagram findings.

claim: Both traveling waves and oscillations result from interrelation between the spiral symmetry-breaking mechanism and the effects of confinement.
source: and we suggest that both traveling waves and oscillations result from interrelation between the spiral symmetry-breaking mechanism and the effects of confinement.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion and interpretation of the findings.
